39: Coffee catering is easy for a client to book and hard to deliver well. Demand comes from companies booking corporate events, trade shows and brand activations, couples planning weddings, and families celebrating at home. On Flashquotes, a booking platform that published data on 25,860 coffee cart bookings from 578 operators, the typical event has about 100 guests and the median booking is $1,040. This plan is for a barista-owner who wants to serve all three with a coffee cart and a portable espresso bar, working from a permitted commissary.
40: The concept is a coffee catering company with two espresso stations: an espresso cart and a portable espresso bar, both carried in an enclosed trailer that the owner's own vehicle tows. The service is hosted: the host pays, and W-2 baristas serve espresso drinks, batch brew, cold brew, milks, syrups and compostable cups. Weekday corporate events are the volume (69.3% of real bookings on Flashquotes are corporate), weddings are the ticket, and private parties fill the rest. Festivals and farmers markets, where each guest pays, are a smaller complement; some festival organizers offer a minimum sales guarantee. The base is a commissary. This is not a coffee shop with a storefront, a food truck on a daily route or a bar that sells espresso martinis, which needs a license.
41: The total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} in startup costs plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The heavy lines are the espresso machines ({{inv_espresso}}) and the espresso cart ({{inv_carro}}), followed by the trailer, the portable bar and the launch budget. For reference, cart-king.com puts the cart itself at $4,000-25,000 and a complete single-cart setup at about $16,600-49,000, with $24,000 typical. We do not build or lease a storefront, which keeps the investment far below a coffee shop. We cover it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. A loan of that size is above the $50,000 SBA Microloan cap, so the realistic routes are a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, and no plan can promise a lender's answer.
42: In year 1 we plan {{eventos_a1}} events with an average of {{invitados_evento}} guests at {{precio_invitado}} per guest, excluding sales tax. That adds up to {{ventas_a1}} in revenue, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3 as events grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} and then {{crecimiento_a3}}. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, the lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}}, and the business breaks even at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. Be honest about what this case is: a full-time owner-barista with active corporate sales and two stations, not the average first year. Read these numbers as a well-run target and replace the inputs with your own.
43: The founding team is small. The owner is the lead barista and also sells, buys and drives. A part-time lead barista runs the second station and the second event of the day, event baristas work event by event, and an on-call barista who doubles as the driver covers the peak months. Everyone except the owner is an hourly W-2 employee. That makes {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. Replace this paragraph with your own background: a lender wants to see who has run an espresso bar and who has sold events. The plan shows that a coffee catering company can start without a storefront and with controlled risk, as long as every event is quoted, booked with a retainer and staffed on purpose.
46: Our clients buy an event that runs smoothly, not just coffee. Companies, usually through an office manager or a planner, book weekday corporate events, conferences, trade shows and brand activations. Couples book weddings months ahead, for the cocktail hour or the dessert hour. Families book birthdays, baby and bridal showers and graduations, and festival and farmers market organizers book guest-pay pop-ups. All of them want specialty coffee made to order, no long lines and one team that takes care of everything, from setup to breakdown. The sales cycle differs: couples book once, while companies reorder.
47: Our value proposition rests on three pillars. First, the offer: "unlimited made-to-order espresso drinks during your booked service window," as one operator puts it (iconcoffeecart.com), with oat milk included, as Houston Coffee Cart does on Zola. Signature and seasonal drinks and house-made syrups give the menu a personality. Second, the brand: branded cups and latte printing turn a corporate event into a brand activation, and setup takes about one hour (coffeecartboys.com). Third, simplicity: the cart is self-contained, so no plumbing connection is required, and the client gets one quote with the baristas, the setup and the cleanup included. Each pillar lets us compete on the experience and stay out of a price war over the cheapest cup.
48: We quote by the guest, excluding sales tax and with the baristas included, and the average is {{precio_invitado}}. With {{invitados_evento}} guests per event, the average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}, between the Flashquotes median of $1,040 and its 75th percentile of $1,697. Coffee bar packages are {{cuota_paquetes_pct}} of sales, and the rest are add-ons such as extra hours, branded cups and latte printing, pastries from a licensed bakery and travel fees. A retainer of 30-50% holds the date and the balance is due 14 days before (grindkit.app); a travel fee applies beyond a free radius. The service charge is part of our price. A voluntary gratuity is not, and it belongs to the team.
49: We compete against four alternatives. Other coffee carts and coffee trucks sell a similar experience, and the best of them are booked on the same dates we want. Neighborhood coffee shops that cater have a name but serve their own counter first. General caterers add coffee as one more item, often from a thermos. Self-serve coffee at hotels wins on price and loses on service. We place ourselves in the gap: two stations that make about 100 drinks an hour with two baristas, oat milk included, and a focus on weekday corporate events. We do not compete on price: on Flashquotes, the lowest tenth of bookings goes for $612 or less.
50: Three formats let the client match the event to the budget: a full-service espresso bar with baristas (a 2-hour service is the standard, 55.3% of Flashquotes bookings), a self-serve coffee station or drop-off of cold brew, and a guest-pay pop-up with a minimum sales guarantee. The short menu has espresso, americano, latte, cappuccino, flat white, mocha, chai latte, hot chocolate, cold brew, batch brew and a signature drink, and add-ons go on top. We sell it for corporate events, weddings, showers, birthdays, festivals and farmers markets. The pricing calculator turns your costs into a quote per guest, per service hour and per drink.
53: Demand for coffee catering comes from the buyer, and the useful measure is local. Check the demand in your own area: a keyword tool such as Google Keyword Planner shows how many people around you search for terms like "coffee catering" or "coffee cart for events." These are people who want to hire a coffee service, not start one. We do not quote a market size, because every source defines it differently. What matters for you is how many offices, venues and wedding planners sit within an hour of your commissary, and how many of them already book coffee for their events.
54: Private clients compare photos, reviews and the price before they ask for a quote. As a reference, Flashquotes (25,860 bookings from 578 operators) shows a median coffee cart booking of $1,040, with the middle half between $764 and $1,697 and a typical event of 100 guests. By size, the price per guest is about $38 under 50 guests, $18 from 50 to 99 and $13 from 100 to 249. GrindKit lists $700 for 50 guests and $950 for 100 guests for a 2-hour hosted service. Operators we read range from $400 to $1,800: Icon starts at $850, Houston Coffee Cart lists $1,000-1,500 and Big Dipper falls inside that band.
55: Corporate clients buy on a different logic, and they are most of the volume: 69.3% of bookings on Flashquotes are corporate, on weekdays (offices, conferences, trade shows and brand activations), and about 31% fall on weekends, mostly weddings and private parties. The buyer is usually an office manager or a planner who needs a reliable vendor and an invoice that fits company rules. As a reference, a premium wedding or a brand activation runs $1,697-3,000, a wedding cart with a barista runs $700-1,800 in 2026 wedding guides, and multi-day corporate contracts run $3,000-10,000.
56: The example mix is a kit estimate, not market data. Of {{eventos_a1}} events, 110 are corporate events of about 90 guests, 30 are weddings of about 130, 20 are private parties and showers of about 45 and 10 are festival or market days of about 150 drinks, some with a minimum sales guarantee. The plan does not price each type separately: it models one blended average of {{precio_invitado}} per guest across that mix, which gives {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue. Typical prices per guest run lower for large corporate groups and higher for small private parties. Corporate events are about 65% of the events. The calendar is uneven too. The example opens in March, so Month 1 is March, with peaks in March, May and December, and July books about a third of December on Flashquotes. The lowest cash balance falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} at {{saldo_minimo}}. Rotate the curve to your opening month.
57: A few trends are worth watching without leaning on numbers we cannot source. Plant-based milks keep growing, and oat milk is now often included. Cold brew and seasonal drinks sell well, brands want branded cups and latte printing, and couples add coffee stations to weddings alongside the dessert table.
58: Demand has risks the plan should name. Corporate events are about 65% of the events, so a few budget cuts can leave a gap. The season dips in summer: July is only 3.8% of coffee cart bookings. Only 20-30% of quotes become bookings (Flashquotes). And {{eventos_a1}} events a year is the pace of a full-time owner-barista with active corporate sales, not of a typical first year, which is slower. Flashquotes shows about 15 bookings per operator per year on its own platform only, which is not an operator's total. The pessimistic scenario shows the hit: {{pesimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}.
61: Before you set a price, map who competes with you within an hour of your commissary. The list usually includes other coffee carts and mobile espresso bars (Coffee Cart Boys, Icon, Big Dipper and Houston Coffee Cart are examples we read), coffee trucks and trailers, coffee shops that cater, the coffee served by general caterers and self-serve coffee at hotels. Request quotes and read their reviews on Google, The Knot and Zola.
62: Porter's five forces look like this for a coffee catering company. Supplier power is low to moderate: many roasters and dairies compete for your order, although a single supplier can raise your costs. Buyer power is moderate to high: corporate clients compare quotes per booking, but a good tasting and a clear proposal build loyalty. The threat of substitutes is real: a caterer's thermos coffee or a coffee shop that delivers can replace you on a lower budget. Rivalry peaks in the weeks around March, May and December, when everyone chases the same dates. The threat of new entrants is moderate: a cart is cheap to start, but serving 100 drinks an hour with two stations, a permitted commissary, a mobile food unit permit and insurance with COIs take planning, and that slows the hobbyists.
63: Direct competitors are coffee carts and mobile espresso bars that serve the same events and the same venues, from weekend operators to full-service companies. Indirect ones are coffee shops that cater, thermos coffee from general caterers and self-serve coffee at hotels. To compare fairly, line up the price per booking and per guest, the hours included, whether oat milk is included or costs extra (Sweet Carolinas, on zola.com, includes oat milk and charges $50 for an additional alternative milk), the free travel radius, and whether the generator is included ("no hidden generator or setup fees," as coffeecartboys.com puts it). Read their reviews on Google, The Knot, Zola and GigSalad. Then decide where you win and put it in one sentence.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash, and both depend on the format. A coffee cart rolls into a ballroom or onto a lawn; cart-king.com puts a complete single-cart setup at about $16,600-49,000. A coffee trailer serves outdoors only and costs about $15,000 to build plus $10,000 to equip, and a coffee truck runs from about $20,000 used to $80,000 custom (greenjoecoffeeschool.com, 2019 prices). All three are mobile food units: you need a permit with a plan review, usually before you buy, and a permitted commissary, and a coffee truck also needs its own registration and commercial auto. This plan picks a cart plus a portable bar carried in an enclosed trailer: two stations that work indoors and outdoors, for far less than a custom coffee truck. Then come power (a two-group machine, about $8,500 at store prices, needs a dedicated 220V circuit or a generator), insurance with COIs for the venues, and the craft: a barista who keeps 50-65 drinks an hour moving.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is speed and consistency: 50-65 drinks an hour per barista, with every drink dialed in. The second is food safety: milk is a TCS food, so keep it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit) and write down the temperature. The third is punctuality at setup: arrive with time to spare, with the outlet confirmed. The fourth is your relationship with office managers, event planners and venues, who send many bookings, and the reviews they read. A small operator that does all four well can take work from larger rivals.
66: The SWOT for this concept looks like this. Strengths: low fixed costs, since you pay {{ocupacion_anual}} a year for a commissary, cart storage and trailer parking instead of a storefront lease, a high gross margin and recurring weekday corporate business. Weaknesses: reliance on a few key people and a summer dip, with capacity of up to {{capacidad_eventos}} events a year on two stations, and dependence on the venue's power. Opportunities: companies that want a regular vendor, venues and planners with preferred vendor lists, and brands that want a branded cup. Threats: a foodborne illness, a late cancellation, an equipment breakdown, corporate budget cuts and cheap competitors.
69: The marketing strategy follows two funnels, plus a channel that runs on referrals. Companies have a short, repeating cycle: a well-run event leads to the next booking and to a referral inside the same office, so you sell actively and aim for recurring weekday bookings. Weddings have a long cycle: the couple finds you online, asks for a quote, attends a tasting and signs months before the date. Private parties travel by referral and marketplaces. Treat each funnel with its own message, and build all three on the same promise: a barista team that arrives on time, serves great espresso and handles everything.
70: Your website is the main sales tool, because clients read it before they call. It should show the packages, "starting at" prices per guest for each type of event, photos of the cart at real events and a short quote form that asks for the date, the venue, the guest count and the service hours. Complete your Google Business Profile and keep collecting reviews, so you show up when someone nearby searches "coffee catering." Instagram posts with latte art and the cart working at real events sell more than any slogan.
71: Directories bring qualified leads when your profile is complete. For weddings, The Knot and Zola are where couples compare vendors, read reviews and request quotes. GigSalad, Thumbtack and The Bash suit private parties, where you pay for leads or a commission and need to reply fast. Add LinkedIn and direct outreach to office managers and planners. Some venues charge an outside vendor fee, so price it into the quote before you accept. Measure the cost per booking won in each channel, use the directories to win new clients and invite repeat clients to book directly.
72: Direct selling works if you are willing to go out and meet people. Start with venues and hotels, event planners, office managers and coworking spaces in your area, and bring a one-page sheet with the packages and a starting price per guest. Ask to be added to a venue's preferred vendor list: a venue that recommends you sends bookings at no advertising cost. Reach out to the organizers of festivals and farmers markets too, for guest-pay pop-ups. Offer a free hour of espresso at an open house for the planners who book the most. Bridal shows let you meet couples in person. After every visit, send an email and set a reminder. A steady rhythm of small contacts each week works better than one big campaign.
73: The tasting is the step closest to the sale, so budget it as a line in the plan (the P&L carries it as tastings for prospects). Offer a corporate open house or a tasting for couples, with a printed proposal. You can charge for it and credit it to the booking if the client signs. The proposal lists the menu, the service hours, the baristas, the price per guest and the final guest count date. The process is quote, contract, then a retainer that holds the date. Companies often pay on net 30 terms, while the workbook assumes you collect in {{cobro_dias}} days on average, since private clients pay before the date. Follow up within a day.
74: The best marketing comes after the event. Ask for a Google review within a few days, while the client still remembers the event, and send a short thank-you with a photo if they agree. Companies that reorder get a simple process: their usual order saved and one named contact. Ask happy clients to introduce you to a colleague who books team events or a friend planning a celebration, and thank them with a small gesture. Planners who recommend you deserve a follow-up too. A referral habit run well costs less than any new lead.
75: The example reserves {{marketing_anual}} a year for marketing, mostly for The Knot and Zola listings, GigSalad, Thumbtack and The Bash leads, photography and bridal shows, plus the launch budget, which is already in the investment. Record where each lead comes from (website, directory, venue, planner or referral) and calculate the marketing cost per event won. If a channel wins events at a lower cost, it gets more budget; if not, drop it. Review the numbers every quarter and adjust.
